candidates.headline: Auto-regressive decode regularity does not guarantee one-page-group-per-iteration overlap under multi-token speculation or chunked prefill.
candidates.claim: vAttention's one-page-group-per-iteration overlap does not guarantee hidden mapping latency if decode regularity changes to multi-token speculation or chunked prefill.
candidates.paper_fact: For a request in the decode phase, the number of new page-groups required is at most one per virtual tensor. This is because each iteration produces only one output token for a request.
candidates.premise: Speculative decoding can produce multiple tokens per iteration, and chunked prefill maps many prompt tokens at once.
candidates.inference: The overlap sizing and deferred reclamation tuned for one token per decode iteration may not cover the larger per-iteration mapping demand.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If speculative decoding or larger chunked prefill is used, VMM mapping latency may appear in the critical path unless page-group allocation is resized or prefetched.
candidates.critical_link: The critical link is per-iteration demand predictability and the one-token growth assumption; overlap is sized to at most one new page-group per virtual tensor per decode iteration.

candidates.headline: Deferred reclamation does not imply or guarantee net throughput gain.
candidates.claim: Reusing a completed request's page-groups can avoid prefill allocation latency, but retaining those physical pages can reduce the memory available for active requests, so deferred reclamation does not by itself guarantee higher end-to-end throughput.
candidates.paper_fact: vAttention simply defers the reclamation of R1’s page-groups (Figure 5(d)) and assigns R1’s reqId to R2.
candidates.premise: GPU physical memory is finite, and KV-cache page-groups retained for future reuse are not available to increase the current batch size or to admit other requests.
candidates.inference: If retained pages reduce the maximum batch size or force preemption, the throughput lost from lower concurrency can exceed the prefill-latency savings from avoiding page mapping.
candidates.toy_example: Not a measurement: if retaining pages for reuse prevents one additional request from fitting in the active batch, the saved mapping time may be smaller than the lost decode throughput from that request.
candidates.conditional_consequence: Under high memory pressure or high request churn with large active batches, deferred reclamation can lower throughput even though it reduces allocation calls in prefill.
candidates.critical_link: The retained page-groups must materially reduce free physical memory and batch capacity, and the saved allocation latency must be smaller than the throughput cost of reduced concurrency.

candidates.headline: Dense-attention evidence does not imply or guarantee no TLB thrashing for irregular or sparse attention
candidates.claim: The paper's finding that 64KB pages do not degrade evaluated attention kernels and show no evidence of TLB thrashing is limited to regular dense attention and hand-tuned kernels; it does not guarantee the same for irregular or sparse attention.
candidates.paper_fact: We attribute this to the regular computation pattern of the attention operator as well as the hand-tuned implementations that explicitly try to avoid irregular memory accesses.
candidates.premise: TLB performance depends on access locality and working-set size; smaller pages generally require more translations and can thrash when accesses are irregular or sparse.
candidates.inference: If attention access becomes irregular or sparse, the 64KB page mechanism may incur TLB misses that were not observed in the paper's dense-attention experiments.
candidates.toy_example: Toy example, not a measurement: a sparse kernel touching one token per 64KB page could require many TLB entries, but this is illustrative only.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If deployed with sparse or irregular attention kernels, the small-page benefit may be offset by TLB overhead, so page size should be re-evaluated.

candidates.headline: Preallocating physical pages does not guarantee forward progress under memory pressure
candidates.claim: vAttention's preallocated page pool plus failure/preemption policy can make some request progress, but it does not guarantee high aggregate goodput or bounded wasted work when memory pressure triggers preemption.
candidates.paper_fact: If vAttention cannot satisfy the memory demand, it returns with a failure in response to which a serving framework can preempt one or more requests to allow forward progress
candidates.premise: Preemption is a recovery action: it frees memory by dropping or delaying a request, and the dropped request's KV cache and generated tokens are typically lost or must be recomputed.

candidates.headline: Request-level reqId indexing conflicts with attention kernels that require Q and KV batch dimensions to match
candidates.claim: ReqId slots create holes when requests exit, so reqId indexing does not by itself guarantee compatibility with attention kernels that expect the query batch and KV cache batch to have the same size and order.
candidates.paper_fact: When a request from somewhere in the middle of a batch exits, it creates an unused hole in the virtual tensors of KV cache. This layout is not supported by implementations that expect the query (Q) and KV cache to be of the same size in batch (𝐵) dimension.
candidates.premise: Many attention kernels assume aligned batch dimensions or a direct batch-index correspondence between Q and KV; a hole in the KV slot array breaks that correspondence unless the kernel supports an explicit mapping or the system compacts/remaps.
candidates.inference: The reqId design relies on cache_batch_idx or equivalent remapping to handle mid-batch exits; without such kernel support, holes from reqId slots force compaction or kernel changes.
candidates.toy_example: Not a measurement: with B=4 and reqIds 0,1,2 active, if reqId 1 exits, Q has 3 rows but the KV virtual tensor still has 4 slots; a kernel without cache_batch_idx cannot map Q row 2 to KV slot 2 unless the system remaps or compacts.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If the serving stack uses an attention kernel that lacks cache_batch_idx or arbitrary Q-to-KV batch mapping, then continuous batching with reqId holes will require compaction, kernel modification, or avoidance of mid-batch exits.
candidates.critical_link: The paper explicitly says the hole layout is unsupported by implementations expecting equal Q and KV batch sizes, and it relies on FlashAttention’s cache_batch_idx to map Q tensors to reqId-based KV slots.

candidates.headline: Ensuring enough mapped pages before kernel dispatch does not imply or guarantee hidden step latency.
candidates.claim: The step API's guarantee that physical pages are mapped up to each active request's current context length is a backing/correctness guarantee; it does not by itself guarantee that the mapping work is off the critical path or that an iteration will avoid latency spikes.
candidates.paper_fact: growing the KV cache of one request by new page-groups (two per layer) adds about 5 millisecond latency to the corresponding iteration. The latency overhead grows proportional to the number of requests that need new page-groups in a given iteration.
candidates.premise: CUDA VMM mapping calls have nonzero latency; if the framework invokes step synchronously before dispatching the first kernel, the mapping time is on the iteration's critical path unless it is overlapped or avoided.
candidates.inference: A step call can return with enough pages mapped and still delay kernel dispatch when many requests need new page-groups and the mapping is not overlapped. The paper's latency hiding comes from separate optimizations such as a background thread, eager allocation, and deferred reclamation, not from the step API's mapping guarantee alone.
candidates.toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): if many decode requests each need a new page-group and each mapping costs tens of microseconds per layer, a synchronous step can add milliseconds before the kernel starts.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If many active requests need new page-groups in the same iteration and allocation is synchronous or the background thread cannot keep up, then step latency can scale with batch and become visible in iteration latency.
candidates.critical_link: The step API ensures backing before dispatch; latency hiding depends on when and how the mapping is performed relative to compute, not on the fact that pages are mapped.
